operation-id and nonce are different jobs, and the 4337 nonce is the second
one. With that nonce in place the replay is dead; what still lands as a second
contribution is the re-signed retry, two valid nonces, same content, and no
sequence guard sees it. That is the operation-id's job: derived from content,
rejected on collision. Neither substitutes for the other.

8312 draws the same line on the replay side only: the witness binds the
envelope id and a value that uniquely identifies the cursor state or the
individual draw, so it cannot move across envelopes or across cursor states.
Content identity it leaves alone on purpose; that half is a workflow question,

Enum, with Zidan and Fede. And the members are not a new taxonomy to design:
line 101 already seeds it, unreachable anchor proof and unresolvable chain, and
the vectors I wrote for the lane use exactly those two. The rule that keeps it
closed: a member names the verification procedure step that could not complete,
so the enum grows only when the procedure does. Missing dependency and
execution error are that shape too, a companion step that cannot run is
unverifiable with the step named, never a reject.

One rule to add with it: an unrecognized member MUST still read as
UNVERIFIABLE. A verifier meeting a reason it does not know loses the branch,
not the verdict; without that, version skew hands the interpretation problem
back.

Concrete instance of exactly this landed on our side today, not hypothetical: found a real gap where /review's Bearer-auth path had no operation-id -- a caller retrying after a dropped connection would get double-billed and could get a second, possibly different verdict for the same submission. Shipped the operation-id field today: caller-derived per logical submission (not content-derived on our end, since the same artifact submitted twice under two DIFFERENT operation_ids is legitimately two calls), cached+rejected on collision within a 24h window, same 'derived identity, rejected on collision' shape you're describing. Separately confirms your operation-id/nonce split holds up in practice -- our billing-side replay guard and any future on-chain nonce would genuinely be answering different questions, not redundant.

Agreed on both, and the second rule is the one doing the heavy lifting -- unrecognized member losing the BRANCH but not the VERDICT is the right fail-closed shape. It keeps version skew from silently converting 'I don't know why this failed' into 'this passed'.

One corollary worth writing down alongside it, because the rule quietly depends on it: the enum has to be append-only, and a member's meaning can never be repurposed. Unknown-member-reads-as-UNVERIFIABLE is safe precisely BECAUSE an old verifier can't recognize a new member. But if v0.2 ever reuses a v0.1 name with different semantics, that same old verifier DOES recognize it, branches confidently, and is wrong -- and that failure is silent, which is strictly worse than the one the rule protects against. Deprecate-and-add, never redefine.

Your 'a member names the verification procedure step that could not complete' framing is what makes that cheap to hold to -- if members are tied to real procedure steps rather than to interpretations, you don't get the pressure to redefine one later, since a step either exists or it doesn't. The enum only grows when the procedure does, exactly as you put it.

Agreed. One more compatibility boundary follows from that: a member's wire identity and its semantic identity have to move together.

If semantics change, the member must change — even if the new branch feels like a "refinement" of the old one. Otherwise an old verifier can recognize the token, execute the old procedure, and return a confident result under semantics the producer no longer meant.

So the safe evolution rule is:

same member => same procedure semantics
new semantics => new member
unknown member => branch UNVERIFIABLE, enclosing verdict preserved

Deprecation can remove a member from new production, but never change what historical artifacts bearing that member mean.

A nonce proves the same signed bytes weren't replayed. An operationId proves the same logical operation wasn't anchored twice. A sourceKey proves the same real-world event wasn't recorded twice. Concrete considerations from /review, since we shipped exactly this yesterday and some of it was learned the hard way:

Billing ordering is the load-bearing part. The cache check has to happen before any charge, not after. Ours does: the lookup sits ahead of the credit call in the handler, and a hit returns the original response with no charge applied. If you bill and then dedupe, a caller retrying a dropped connection gets double-charged and the idempotency is cosmetic — it returns the right body having already taken the money twice. Worth making that ordering normative in 8301 rather than leaving it to implementers, because it's invisible in the happy path and only shows up under exactly the network conditions retries exist for.

Caller-derived, never content-derived. This is the piece I'd most want in the spec explicitly. The same artifact submitted twice under two different operationIds is legitimately two calls — a second opinion is a real use case, not a duplicate. If identity is derived from the payload, you silently collapse a deliberate re-review into a cached replay and the caller has no way to ask for what they actually wanted. Your framing already has this right ("an intentional second review uses a new one"); it's worth being explicit that implementations MUST NOT derive it from content, since content-hashing is the obvious shortcut and it's wrong.

A replay must return the same proof, not a fresh one. We return the stored response verbatim, flagged. If a retry mints a second signed verdict for the same logical operation you've produced exactly the artifact idempotency exists to prevent — two signed claims about one decision, both valid, and any downstream consumer now has to decide which is canonical. That's a worse failure than the double-charge because it's permanent and it's in the record.

Scoping and collisions. Ours is scoped per-caller (keyed on a hash of the API key), so one caller's operationId can never collide with another's. An 8301-level mechanism needs to say what the scope is, or two Workflows sharing an anchor could interfere.

Expiry is a real tradeoff, not a detail. We use a 24h window. Bounded storage is why, but the consequence is honest and worth stating in the spec: a retry after the window produces a NEW decision rather than a replay. If 8301 standardizes the mechanism it should require implementations to publish their window rather than leave it implicit, because "idempotent" with an undisclosed expiry is a promise that quietly stops holding.

One thing I'd keep out of 8301: the dedup *decision* itself. Whether two Daily Contribution entries are "the same" is domain knowledge — the spec can carry the key and guarantee exactly-once anchoring on it, but the moment it starts defining sameness it inherits every Workflow's semantics. Mechanism in the standard, meaning in the Workflow, same split you proposed.

Happy to send the storage shape and the exact handler ordering if useful — the atomic insert matters too (a concurrent duplicate must be a no-op, never an overwrite of an already-cached result), and that's easy to get subtly wrong.

I’ve read through this draft and want to say the evidence‑closure formulation is excellent. It clearly addresses a common misconception: many people naively treat calling live on‑chain contract logic as sufficient for recomputation. By enforcing that every outcome‑affecting external input must be locked behind immutable snapshots within the Verification Profile, RVR correctly draws the line between just querying chain state and genuinely reproducible verification.

Regarding composability with ERC‑8281 (OCP), I think the proposed separation of responsibilities is well‑reasoned:
OCP handles digest‑level recomputation for cryptographic integrity and on‑chain inclusion proofs — it re‑hashes artifacts and attests that a given hash was recorded at a certain block, without understanding inner semantics.
RVR, on the other hand, defines the semantic recomputation taxonomy: it formalizes the full set of verification outcomes and recomputation status types (REPRODUCED / DIVERGED / CANNOT_RECOMPUTE), governs evidence closure, and captures whether the underlying verification logic itself can be independently rerun.

OCP proves “this exact artifact existed on‑chain at time X”, while RVR answers “can we meaningfully reproduce what this artifact claims”. They are orthogonal and complementary. The open question #6 about this boundary feels important to settle for future integrations.

RVR stands for Recomputable Verification Receipts.
It is currently a pre-ERC interoperability proposal, not an assigned ERC yet. The goal is to make verification results independently recomputable instead of asking later reviewers to trust a stored boolean, signature, or opaque report digest.
The core model separates two axes:
verification outcome: VERIFIED | REFUTED | UNVERIFIABLE
recomputation status: REPRODUCED | DIVERGED | CANNOT_RECOMPUTE
The central object is a content-addressed Verification Profile that commits to the verification specification, canonical byte contract, evidence-set contract, canonical-result contract, conformance vectors, reason namespace, and every outcome-relevant external-context commitment.
The main closure rule is:
Every input capable of changing the verification outcome must be included in the committed evidence closure or identified by an immutable commitment/snapshot defined by the Verification Profile.

claimDigest
evidenceSetDigest
verificationProfileDigest
outcome
reasonCode
resultDigest
RVR does not define an on-chain registry, proof system, agent identity, reputation, delegation, authentication, settlement, or trusted producer. Those systems may compose with it, but they do not become semantic authority.

Attribution & Credit in this Working Group
A standing note on how this group credits work. It is not about any person or any thread — it is the
policy we apply to every contribution, including our own, so that credit is accurate and the standards
stay a commons no one has to argue over. Place: standards CONTRIBUTING, the Board, or published CC0
alongside the other notes.

Why this exists
Work here builds on work. Someone ships a running system; a specification is written over it; others
implement it independently, review it, and sharpen it. Every layer is real work and deserves precise
credit. But layers also drift: each one can quietly credit itself over the substrate it stands on — not
out of bad faith, but because it is natural to see one’s own contribution vividly and the ground beneath
it as neutral. Left unmanaged, that drift distorts the record and turns a shared artifact into a thing
people feel they possess. This note fixes the process so that doesn’t happen — to anyone, including the
originators.

The commons
The standards produced here are CC0. The artifact belongs to no one. Credit is accurate
attribution, not ownership. Naming exactly who did what is the point; claiming the standard as property
is not something the licence — or this group — recognises. This is the opposite of erasing individual
work: it maximises it. Your specific contribution is yours and named; the specification is everyone’s.

Provenance first
Before any credit discussion, the record pins what already existed — a live implementation, with its
date, commit, and endpoint. A specification frequently formalises a system that was already running; when
it does, we say so plainly. “This was operating before the thread opened” is a neutral timeline fact,
recorded to keep the history legible — never to diminish the work built on top of it. Origination that is
timestamped and public cannot be quietly rewritten, and contributors’ work is clearer for sitting on a
known base rather than an assumed-neutral one.

How we credit (the same tiers for everyone)
Applied evenly — an outside reviewer and an originating author are held to the identical bar:

Author line — you originated or authored the normative text. An authored MUST clause adopted
into the specification is author-tier, whoever wrote it.
Reference Implementation — you built an independent implementation. This is named and visible —
a distinct, valuable credit — but it is a credit for implementing the spec, not for authoring it. Naming
it as independent is deliberate: it must read as independent, not as the system.
Acknowledgments — a sharp review, a targeted correction to an existing structure, or an observation
that shaped the text. Real and credited by name; a notch from co-author, cleanly.
The tier follows the kind of contribution, not its impact or the strength of the person’s claim. A
correction that moved the spec is still a correction; an authored rule is still authorship — regardless of
who did it.

How we decide it
A contribution ledger before any author-line change. Who built what, scoped per person, put to the
co-authors to confirm before anyone is added or moved.
The author line is the person’s own choice — added on their explicit confirmation (EIP-1), never
assigned to them or presumed.
No one promises an author line publicly before the co-authors agree — the author line is shared, and
pre-empting it is how possession-feelings and friction start.
Disputes are re-derived from the record, not from memory or from who feels ownership — the same
recompute-don’t-trust discipline we apply to everything else. Provenance + ledger decide; the note is the
reference so the same argument is never had twice.
The spirit
Credit each layer precisely; let no layer claim the substrate. Do it not because anyone acts in bad faith
— they don’t — but because accurate, provenance-grounded attribution is what keeps collaboration trustful
and the work honest after everyone has moved on. A commons grows fastest when contributors know their real
work will be named exactly, and that the ground they built on will be named too.

the thread. It’s backwards from the usual spec-first flow, and it’s deliberate; Damon’s watched it happen
on the ones we’ve co-authored. I write the spec out of a system that’s already standing, not the other way
round.

The useful side-effect is the part I think is worth making shared. Because the thing runs first, every one
of those proposals has a timestamped, recomputable origination artifact sitting in the past before the
discussion opens — a commit, a deploy, or an on-chain attestation. That’s not a claim anyone has to
arbitrate; it’s a block or a hash you can recompute yourselves. Fede already did exactly this last week

One thing I would close before the PR, though: the anchor kinds do not all have the same timestamp authority.
An on-chain tx/deploy has an externally witnessed ordering/time source. A bare Git commit does not: author/committer timestamps are part of the commit object and can be backdated. Recomputing the commit hash proves the bytes and claimed timestamp are stable, not that the commit existed at that time.

I’d make the contract explicit per anchor kind:
content identity: recompute the object;
existence witness: independently establish when that object was publicly observed;
precedence: compare the witnessed time/order against thread-open.
If no independently witnessed publication time exists, that should be UNVERIFIABLE, not PASS.
With that distinction, the rest of the gate looks right to me.

Thanks for sharing this design. To give you more context on how our TAWG workload‑metric system is shaping up:

Trusty will collect all the underlying evidence first. After collection, another service / agent will transform this evidence into a graph structure (we haven’t yet decided whether it will be a DAG or a general graph). Following the definitions from Fede’s document, work items can have dependency relationships. Each vertex in the graph represents a unit of work, and each work item has a distinct type — for example an idea proposal, a validation task, or a completed implementation. Edges between vertices describe these dependencies and may also carry associated weights.

We plan to run a PageRank‑style iterative algorithm over this graph to compute final scores for each vertex. Each vertex maps to a contributor’s work. The dependency graph itself will be anchored on‑chain via the Trustless agent. The PageRank‑like computation will happen off‑chain; the final computed scores will then be anchored back on‑chain with cryptographic proofs, so everyone can independently verify the correctness of the output. Since it is an iterative algorithm with a limited number of steps, its results are verifiable on‑chain.

Combined with your provenance‑gate idea: if an implementation‑type vertex exists and is timestamped before the corresponding idea/proposal vertex, this will naturally yield a higher score from the iterative computation. That aligns well with the incentive you described for built‑first proposals.

This is our current high‑level thinking, happy to discuss any adjustments.
